text: You have passed the same beggar at the inner gate every day for years. Men carry him there each morning. You do not know his name.
“It must be his angel,” you hear yourself say. Rhoda looks at you as if you had struck her.
Joy. The angels sang it, and the shepherds went back praising God. I am still pondering it.
speaker: Mary, the mother of Jesus

text: He told me to say nothing. I went to the priest, as he said. And then I told everyone else. Could you have kept quiet?
speaker: A man who was a leper

text: Her house is the largest you have entered since Caesarea. On the threshold you think of Peter and the sheet let down from heaven, and you go in.

“If God shows no favoritism, who else have I been calling unclean?” (Acts 10:28, 34)

The Greeks of Antioch, who believed and turned to the Lord. (Acts 11:20–21)
In the shade of a portico, two of your teachers speak quietly with a priest of the high priest’s family. When they see you, they stop.
When the teaching ends, he does not go back toward the town. He walks along the shore, straight toward the toll booth.
Then the emperor wanted everyone counted. Joseph was of David’s house, so we had to go to David’s town. I was very near my time.
speaker: Mary, the mother of Jesus

text: You pull a hanging behind them and stand in front of it, as if you were only a guest who had been asleep.
There was no room, so I laid him where the animals ate. The Lord of everything, in a feeding trough. I counted his fingers.
speaker: Mary, the mother of Jesus

text:
“What did Simeon mean: “a sword will pierce through your own soul”?” (Luke 2:35)

Mary stood by the cross of her son (John 19:25). Simeon’s word had come true: the sword was this. (John 19:25; Luke 2:35)

At the harbor John Mark says he is going home. Paul says nothing, and his silence is louder than anything he could have said. Barnabas asks whether you will go on with them, up into the mountains. You do.
It is nearly dawn in Ephesus. The others have gone home. The girl is still reading to you, and there is only a little of the scroll left in her right hand.

“Acts ends with Paul teaching “without hindrance,” and does not say what happened next. Why might Luke end there?” (Acts 28:30–31)

Because the story was never Paul’s to finish. He wrote from his last prison: “God’s word isn’t chained.” (2 Timothy 2:9)
You walked north for a week to warn the believers in Damascus that Saul was coming with letters. You are too late, though not in the way you feared.
You tell him what Isaiah promised: that God will give eunuchs who keep his covenant a place in his house, and a name better than sons and daughters. His eyes fill.
You won’t get in that way, daughter. Squeeze in by the door with the women of the house; you will see from there.
speaker: Someone in the crowd
